title: A multi-scale information geometry reveals the structure of mutual information in neural populations
claim: Quantities that look identical under a local measure diverge once multi-scale structure is considered, exposing hidden differences in information content.
layout: 6 panels in two rows; tuning curves, then Fisher, scale heatmaps, multi-scale result
description: Six small plots, labelled A to F, built on a one-dimensional stimulus x. The top row has two tuning curves. Panel A is a blue bell-shaped curve and panel B is an orange monotonic sigmoid-like curve. Panel C shows Fisher information J(x) for both curves. The blue and orange lines overlap exactly as a double-peaked curve, shown as a dashed overlay. The bottom row has two heatmaps, D and E, showing contribution at diffusion scale t on a log axis against x. They use a black-purple-orange-yellow colormap with a shared colorbar. The bell-shaped map is dimmer and splits into two lobes. The monotonic map is brighter with a hot central blob. Panel F plots the multi-scale Fisher G(x), with the orange monotonic curve clearly above the blue bell-shaped curve. Blue and orange colour-code the two tuning curves across all panels.
caption: Fisher and multi-scale Fisher for a one-dimensional stimulus. (A–B) Bell-shaped and monotonic tuning curves (E[r | x] = f(x)) for a single neuron with stimulus-independent Gaussian noise, encoding a scalar stimulus x with uniform prior. (C) The Fisher information is identical for both tuning curves, since they share the same local gradient magnitude and Gaussian noise variance. (D–E) Contribution at each diffusion scale, [ϕt ∗Jt](x) δt, to the multi-scale Fisher, for the bell-shaped (D) and monotonic (E) tuning curves. (F) The multi-scale Fisher is larger everywhere for the monotonic tuning curve, reflecting that it encodes strictly more mutual information.
abstract: Understanding how neural population responses represent sensory information is a central problem in systems neuroscience. One approach is to define a representational geometry on stimulus space in which distances reflect how reliably stimuli can be distinguished from neural activity. However, different constructions of these distances can lead to qualitatively different conclusions about the neural code. Here, we show that a unique Riemannian representational geometry emerges from first principles governing how distances contract as stimulus resolution is lost through coarse-graining. This results in a multi-scale extension of the Fisher information metric, capturing encoding structure from fine stimulus details to coarse global distinctions. The resulting geometry is exactly related to the mutual information encoded by the population: well-encoded stimulus directions (those contributing more to mutual information) are expanded, whereas poorly encoded directions are contracted. The metric tensor can be estimated using diffusion models, making the framework practical for large neural populations and high-dimensional stimuli. Applied to visual cortical responses to natural images, the eigenvectors of the metric tensor identify stimulus variations that contribute most to the encoded stimulus information, yielding interpretable features that are robust to modelling choices. Together, these results provide a principled, information-theoretic framework for characterising neural population codes.
